title: A billionaire tried to buy my family's tiny cabin for $2 million. We refused — until we found what was buried under the porch (PART 2)

blocks.text: …a rare-earth deposit the federal government mapped in 1974. And your client has known about it for five years."
The lawyer tried to laugh it off. "That's a fifty-year-old map."
"Then why does your client want forty acres of rocks so badly?" I asked.
He didn't have an answer. He packed up his briefcase and left without another word.

I spent the next week finding out what my grandfather had hidden. In 1974, a federal geological survey team asked his permission to drill test wells along our creek. He agreed. The crates held their core samples, and the survey showed a large deposit of rare-earth minerals, the kind used in electric car batteries and smartphones, eighty feet below the creek bed. When the team told my grandfather a mining company would pay a fortune for it, he asked what would happen to the creek.
They told him the truth: it would be gone.

So he kept the samples, refused every offer, and never told anyone, not even my dad. The survey was never published because the landowner wouldn't allow further work. The developer had found an old reference to it in a government archive five years ago. That's when the shell companies started calling.

A mineral rights attorney told me the deposit could be worth far more than two million dollars. But mining it would mean destroying the creek, the timber, and the cabin my great-grandfather built by hand.

I thought about my grandfather for a long time. Then I called a land trust instead. They bought a conservation easement on the property, which permanently prevents mining or development there. The payment covered every one of my dad's medical bills, with enough left over to fix the porch properly.
The core samples are now at the state university's geology department. The professor there told me they're the best-preserved samples from that survey anywhere in the country.
I hung my grandfather's laminated map above the fireplace in the cabin. Underneath it, I wrote what my dad always said: "Some things aren't for sale."
